Capacity building
Capacity building for construction workers is often a component of the project I have been involved in. I have organized and run courses on different topics related to construction and disaster preparedness. The key challenge in this type of activities is to find ways to communicate practical and theoretical knowledge to a wide and diverse audience. It is also essential to commmunicate the reasons behind guidelines and regulations so that workers do not only adopt them but understand their rationale.

title: Water Security as a diagram
text:
When working at Newcastle University on Water Security, I felt the complexity of that concept could be reduced to a simpler form taking inspiration from system diagrams. The idea was to place 3 elements at the center of the diagram. Nature(N), Population (P) mediated by infrastructure (I). Additionally these 3 elements would have close relation to enabling factors such as governance (G) and resources (R). This part of the diagram represent the system at a local level. This can be thought as a region, village, basin, it would depend on local conditions.
This “local system” would then have external stressors such as climate change (CC), political change (PL), growth (GU) and economic changes (EC).

What is perhaps more interesting is that the relation between these nodes can describe particular situations. For example, nature-population (N-P) represent natural hazards on one way and human threat to the natural environment. Resources given to infrastructure is described by R-I. User behaviours between population and infrastructure (P-I).

To test the diagram, I associated the Sustainable Development Goals with each section of the diagram:

title: How rainy is the rainy season?
text: When planning for construction work, rainfall become a very crucial factor. Data is easily available with month averages but more insights into historical data may be beneficial. I gathered data from Cox Bazaar weather station and did some analysis.

title: How rainy is the rainy season?
text:
Data gathering
Analysis of daily rainy precipitation recorded at Cox’s Bazar weather station, 1970 to 2016. Data source.


Code

library(rbokeh)

## Load data, select station and erase NA
raw <- read.csv("bgd_hist_precipitation.csv")%>%filter(Station=="CoxsBazar")
raw$Date <- as.Date(paste(raw$Year,raw$Month,raw$Day,sep="-"))
raw <- filter(raw,!is.na(raw$Date))

#Create day of the year
raw$DayOfYear <- lubridate::yday(raw$Date)
raw$MonWord<- format(raw$Date, "%h")

# Create timeserie
data_ts <- xts(raw$Rainfall, raw$Date) 

# Compute stats based on DoY
rain_day <- data.frame(rain=raw$Rainfall, day=raw$DayOfYear)
rain_avg <- rain_day %>% group_by(day) %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(rain),
            median= median(rain),
            rain_perc=sum(rain > 0)/length(rain),
            rain_heavy=sum(rain > 80)/length(rain))
# Add months and day
rain_avg$month <- raw[1:366, "Month"]
rain_avg$daymonth <- raw[1:366, "Day"]
rain_avg$monword <- raw[1:366, "MonWord"]


#raw$singleday <- paste(raw$Month,raw$Day,sep="-")
raw$DayOfYear <- lubridate::yday(raw$Date)

##Filter data for Cox bazar
data_cox <- filter(raw, raw$Station=="CoxsBazar")
data_cox <- filter(data_cox,!is.na(data_cox$Date))
data_ts <- xts(raw$Rainfall, raw$Date) 
rain_ts_df <-data.frame(Y=as.matrix(data_ts), date=time(data_ts))

text:
Very happy to have published with Charles Niwagaba and Annika Nordin an article on the risk assessment of wastewater sludge reuse. What we tried to quantify is the risk that consumer and workers would face while using wastewater sludge as a fertiliser. The numercial models that we built suggest that there is significant risk for both categories but also that other source of microbial contamination exist. We are now working on a policy briefing that will give suggestions on how to better address this issue in Uganda.

title: Explaining QMRA
text:
I had the opportunity of being part of risk assessment that used the Quantitative Microbial Risk Assessment (QMRA) framework. As the name already shows, the desire for academic precision creates usability difficulties by non academic.

Considering that some very interesting tools exist such as Idyll and curve note that try provide more interactive ways of engaging with the readers, we have set up a 10 minutes explanation of the QMRA framework1 using Idyll. It is still a draft but maybe is able to communicate the core idea behind the framework. If you have 10 minutes, take a look. The idea behind the presentation is to give a preliminary understanding of the QMRA process to stakeholders that do not have a technical background.
1 Quantitative microbiological risk assessment (QMRA) is the process of estimating the risk from exposure to microorganisms. The process involves measuring known microbial pathogens or indicators and running a Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the risk of transfer. If a dose-response model is available for the microbe, it be used to estimate the probability of infection. QMRA has expanded to be used to estimate microbial risk in many fields, but is particularly important in assessments of food water supply and human faeces/wastewater safety. wikipedia2 An active reader asks questions, considers alternatives, questions assumptions, and even questions the trustworthiness of the author. An active reader tries to generalize specific examples, and devise specific examples for generalities. An active reader doesn’t passively sponge up information, but uses the author’s argument as a springboard for critical thought and deep understanding. From Bret VictorAlong these ideas it is very interesting to read about the idea of the active reader2 as Bret Victor defines it.

title: Different workflows for rapid evidence gathering
text:
Some notes on how to streamline a research on a specific topic on academic literature using few available free tools. Following a driagram of the process





flowchart TB
  A[Research topic] --> B(Keywords)
  B --> C[Lit. search on databases]
  C --> D[Ranking and screening with AS Review]
  D --> E[Analysis]
  E --> F(Revised keyword)
  F --> C
  E --> G(Evidence synthesis)









My initial interest was on trying to understand the impact of healthcare design and nosocomial infections. I started with few quite general keywords: healthcare facility construction nosocomial. This is not the best choice of keywords but it is likely that at the beginning there is a lack of knowledge and terminology.

healthcare-associated epidemiology nosocomial Evidence Based Relationship Between Healthcare Infrastructure and Nosocomial Infections in Romania Enhancing appropriate environmental design in healthcare facilities for the inhibition of nosocomial infection Facility Design and Healthcare-Acquired Infections Surfaces and fomites as a source of healthcare-associated infections




The selected string for research shown above was searched in several databases using the Publish or Perish software1.In Scopus 23 articles were found, in crossreference 1000 articles,in semantic scholar 811 articles adn in PubMed 11.
The separate RIS files were imported in Zotero and a new file with all the results from different searches was exported

1 https://harzing.com/resources/publish-or-perish/tutorial



Screening was done using AS review2 in different steps. At first, article were manually screened. Using the terms “nosocomial AND design” 5 articles out of the 8 proposed were marked as relevant.
Then ASReview started the active learn process on the 1825 papers3 using TF-IDF and Naive Bayes, clustering and dynamic resampling as options.
The model then proposed different papers to be reviewed for relevance. )0 articles were reviewed with 33 found to be relevant. As shown below, the model was suggesting papers with a 30% relevance ( around 3 paper over 10).

The relevant papers (33 then reduced to 30 due to duplication) were then exported.Since this is a manageable number we move to the analysis phase. Another option would be to use this bibliography and repeat from step 3.

2 ASReview, developed at Utrecht University, helps scholars and practitioners to get an overview of the most relevant records for their work.3 see the website for more explanation



A first analysis was done to create word-cloud from the titles of the relevant bibliography, see margin column.

title: Research workflow with rabbit research
text:
Here is another workflow to quickly find and sort out papers related to a single one. I started by selecting an article Decision-making at the sharp end: a survey of literature related to decision-making in humanitarian contexts. I chose this article becasue explores the topic of sensemaking, something that gets overlooked since it is omnipresent in our daily actions.

Using Research Rabbit i could download a set of related papers (546). See details on this publication.
From this step I used a similar process expalained in this post using ASReview

3.I have uploaded the dataset of 546 entries and have given an initial input on 20 papers by tagging them relevant or not. My focus in on sensemaking and decision making in humanitarian context. Papers on social media are discarded as well as those on using technologies unless there is a focus on decision making.

I went through 120 papers of the 546 and stopped when the relevant papers proposed where areound 20-30% as seen below. Then I downloaded the new list of 63 papers.




Here brief text analysis of the exported file based on abstracts.






























The chosen files where imported in research rabbit to be explored again. The same process as from step 2 could be repeated focusing on another article(s). Items could be imported in Zotero if one connects it with Rabbit Research.

I finally asked Perplexity to write a 3 sentences summary of each study. Results below.

Moody experts : How mood and expertise influence judgmental anchoring
This study examines how mood and expertise jointly moderate anchoring effects in decision-making. Results suggest that sad judges show stronger anchoring effects than happy judges, while experts’ information processing may be relatively independent of mood. These findings indicate that positive mood may eliminate the otherwise robust anchoring effect, at least for non-experts.
Challenges in humanitarian information management and exchange: evidence from Haiti
This study analyzes challenges to information flow in the 2010 Haiti earthquake response and their implications for effective humanitarian action. The fragmented nature of the response and use of hierarchical information management models led some observers to label the Haiti response a failure. The paper concludes by offering possible paths for overcoming such challenges and restoring the value of humanitarian information management in relief settings.
https://doi.org/10.1111/disa.12052
Hygiene programming during outbreaks: a qualitative case study of the humanitarian response during the Ebola outbreak in Liberia
This study describes humanitarian perspectives on changing hygiene behaviors during the 2014-2016 Liberian Ebola outbreak. Humanitarians faced challenges in defining which hygiene behaviors to promote and assumed fear and disease awareness would be the most powerful motivators for behavior change. The experiences of humanitarians allowed researchers to identify areas that could be strengthened when designing hygiene programs in future outbreaks.
https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-020-8240-9
Crisis Management in Hindsight: Cognition, Communication, Coordination, and Control
This article argues that cognition is central to performance in emergency management, defined as the capacity to recognize emerging risk and act on that information. The author reframes intergovernmental crisis management as a complex, adaptive system that needs to adjust its performance to fit changing environments. A reframed crisis management system is conceived as a dynamic interorganizational system characterized by four primary decision points: risk detection, interpretation, communication, and collective response mobilization.
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6210.2007.00827.x
Grounded Theory and Sensitizing Concepts
This article examines the relationship between sensitizing concepts and grounded theory in qualitative research. The author illustrates the application of sensitizing concepts in a study of community-based antipoverty projects in Jamaica. The article contains commentary on trustworthiness techniques, the coding process, and the constant comparative method of analysis, as well as a synopsis of study findings.
Optimizing Decision-Making Processes in Times of COVID-19: Using Reflexivity to Counteract Information-Processing Failures
This review outlines how groupthink, narrow focus, and escalation of commitment may pose risks to decision-making processes in handling the COVID-19 crisis. The authors propose group reflexivity as an antidote to these biases and errors in decision-making. They recommend several evidence-based reflexivity tools that could be implemented to counter information-processing errors and improve decision-making processes in uncertain times.
https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.650525
Cognitive biases in humanitarian sensemaking and decision-making lessons from field research
This article identifies biases that matter for humanitarian decision support, reflecting on the role of field-based decision-makers and digital responders. The most important biases are reviewed to provide an assessment of their role in disaster response. Areas particularly sensitive to reinforced biases are identified, as well as areas where digital volunteers can likely help, concluding with an agenda for future research.
https://doi.org/10.1109/cogsima.2016.7497786
Codifying a crisis: progressing from information sharing to distributed decisionâ€making
This paper explains why it is difficult to move from information sharing towards support for distributed decision-making in crisis management. The authors argue that two key processes need to be considered: supporting both the translation of meaning and the transformation of interests between those on the front line and those in the remote response network. Results from analyzing three large-scale emergency response operations in the Netherlands indicate that collaborative decision-making was often hampered by actors limiting themselves to factual information exchange.
https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-5973.12323
Evaluating COVID-19 decision-making in a humanitarian setting: The case study of Somalia
This study evaluated the process of policy and operational decision-making in relation to the COVID-19 response in Somalia, focusing on the use of information and the role of transparency. The researchers found that nearly all actors struggled to make sense of the epidemic’s scale and form an appropriate response. Important aspects of the response suffered from a transparency deficit and would have benefitted from more inclusive decision-making.
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0000192
The Influence of Decision, Environmental and Firm Characteristics on the Rationality of Strategic Decisionâ€Making
This paper develops an integrated model of strategic decision-making rationality, informed by three perspectives that identify decision, environmental, and firm characteristics as influences. Results from a study in Egypt indicate that the rationality of strategic decision-making processes is shaped by variables identified by all three perspectives. The study suggests that the three perspectives do not contribute equally to explaining strategic decision making, and that the national setting is relevant for how decision-makers consider environmental characteristics.
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-6486.2006.00670.x
The Reality of Evidence-based Decision Making in Humanitarian Programming: An Exploratory Study of WASH Programs in Uganda
This research examined factors influencing the use of evidence in decision-making processes for humanitarian WASH interventions in Uganda. Interviewees reported several factors that impede the implementation of evidence-based decision making, including contradictory and non-repeatable evidence, and information not being in an actionable format. The study shows the importance of considering human aspects and organizational settings that limit access to and use of supporting data, information, and evidence.
https://doi.org/10.1109/ghtc46280.2020.9342885
Knowledge creation and reliable decision-making in complex emergencies
This paper examines how knowledge creation and decision-making authority location within relief organizations influence coordination. The study found that relief organizations rely on quality information dissemination between field and headquarters, but reporting from the field is often overloaded with misplaced precision. The creation of ‘collective-meaning structures’ based on reliable information at all decision-making levels is suggested to open the way to decentralization of decision-making to field officers engaged with inter-organizational coordination structures.
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7717.2011.01255.x
Managing cognitive biases during disaster response: the development of an aide memoire
This research sought to improve decision-making quality by developing an aide memoire for managing cognitive biases in emergency management. Based on literature and expert input, nine cognitive biases were identified and translated into a series of questions. The aide memoire can be used to assess available information, intelligence, and decisions, and then determine their meaning in emergency management contexts.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10111-019-00564-5
An Emergency Decision Making Method Based on Prospect Theory for Different Emergency Situations
This study proposes a novel approach based on prospect theory for emergency decision making (EDM) that considers both decision makers’ psychological behavior and different emergency situations. The approach addresses limitations in existing EDM methods by incorporating these factors into the decision-making process. Two examples and related comparisons are provided to illustrate the feasibility and validity of this approach.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s13753-018-0173-x
Making better decisions in groups
This review identifies common problems of decision-making in individuals and groups, guided by a Bayesian framework. The authors highlight the advantages of group decision-making in overcoming biases and searching for good solutions, while also noting that diverse groups face their own challenges. The paper discusses means of managing these pitfalls and makes recommendations on how to make better group decisions.
https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.170193
Risk, uncertainty, and heuristics
This paper distinguishes between risk and uncertainty in business decision-making, associating economic profit with entrepreneurial decisions under fundamental uncertainties. The authors argue that fast-and-frugal heuristics provide robust strategies for performing well under uncertainty, often deliberately ignoring information and using fewer resources. The paper concludes that in an uncertain world, less information often proves to be more effective for decision-making.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2014.02.013
How emergency managers (mis?)interpret forecasts
This study examined how emergency managers interpret forecast information using hypothetical climate, flood, and weather scenarios. The research revealed that even experienced emergency managers take decision shortcuts and make biased choices, similar to the general population. Their choices vary depending on factors such as the format of probabilistic forecasts and whether outcomes are represented as gains or losses.
https://doi.org/10.1111/disa.12293

Visualising complexity
text:
Semantic network
In an article on Water Security(WS) 1 we tried to find a way to compare different definition for the concept and to break down these definitions in parts for comparison. The result is something fairly close to semantic network 2. From the image below one can see for example how the basic meaning is defined differently. looking at L2 and L3 in the image below, it can be observed that the majority of definitions see WS as “access / availability of water in sufficient quantity and quality”. Other definitions frame it using risk concepts and define it as “acceptable risk level / protection from diseases and disasters”. L4 defines the systems that are supported by WS: most mentioned are a health life and ecosystems, followed by economic aspects (livelihood and production). Lastly L5 indicates other limits that should be considered such as sustainability, geographical limitations, costs.
1 https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/14/18/29072 A semantic network, or frame network is a knowledge base that represents semantic relations between concepts in a network. This is often used as a form of knowledge representation. It is a directed or undirected graph consisting of vertices, which represent concepts, and edges, which represent semantic relations between concepts,[1] mapping or connecting semantic fields. A semantic network may be instantiated as, for example, a graph database or a concept map. Typical standardized semantic networks are expressed as semantic triples.(Wikipedia)
